utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that today is Monday, the 18th of May, 2009. I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic; the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer, as well as all his associates; and all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I will first of all read out a short oral decision handed down by the Chamber. Oral decision on how the IC lists should be filed by the Praljak Defence on a regular basis during the testimony of Witness Slobodan Praljak. On the 14th of May, 2009, after an oral request filed by the Prosecution, since no objection was filed by the Praljak Defence, the Trial Chamber granted leave to the Praljak Defence to file, at the beginning of each week, IC lists which it would like to be tendered. The Trial Chamber permitted this for the entire period of the testimony of Slobodan Praljak. Hereby, the Trial Chamber wishes to specify this exceptional amendment of paragraph 32, line 8 of the guide-lines and clarify in which manner the IC lists can be filed by the Praljak Defence. The Trial Chamber invites, first and foremost, the Praljak Defence to file its IC lists at the beginning of each week, thereby identifying the documents that were presented before the list in question was filed which it wishes to tender into evidence. The Trial Chamber recalls, secondly, that the parties shall file their objections at the end of Slobodan Praljak's testimony, and it will rule, therefore, on the admission into evidence presented by the Praljak Defence once Slobodan Praljak's testimony is completed. This is the oral decision that the Trial Chamber's handed down. It is very clear. At the beginning of each week, the Praljak Defence should file its IC list which coincides with the documents that have been shown the previous week. And at the end of Mr. Praljak's testimony, when it is finished, the parties can then make objections if they need to. So this is all very clear, I hope. Ms. Nozica, I am hoping, and am rather impatient about it, that you will be giving us some very good news.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, everybody else in the courtroom. May we go into private session for me to provide the Chamber with the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In open session, Mr. Kovacic, after the oral decision handed down by the Trial Chamber, would you like to say something or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Everything is clear after this decision. We wanted to hear the entire ruling and not just the first part relating to the IC list, but we will tender it within the next five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Before I give the floor back to Mr. Kovacic, Mr. Kovacic, personally, but I think I'm saying this on behalf of my colleagues also, we would like to ask you to be very concise when you answer. I know that it's very difficult, but try to do this, because this has several advantages. And when the Judges put questions, this means that they have more time to put their questions. As you know, the Registrar is the timekeeper of the time the Bench has for putting questions. Fifteen percent of the time is dedicated to questions put by the Bench, which is much more than all the other Trial Chambers that dedicate less than 1 percent of their time to putting questions. This may have to do with different personalities of the Judges sitting on the Bench. Whatever the case may be, please try to be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer your questions. Mr. Kovacic -- Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue discussing the documents, we're still dealing with 3D02633. We left off discussing that document. And I have to correct the transcript of the 14th of May, 2009, on page 92, line 15, where it should have read that the import of diesel fuel into BiH from Croatian ports begins on 3D32-1280. The number on the record was 3D32-1289, so a correction. 1280 instead of 1289. So we've put that right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, although we had almost completed the topic of the import of diesel fuel through Croatian ports, could you look at page 32-1280. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now look at 3D32-1281 and 1282. And for Their Honours, let me say -- and for the Prosecutor as well, that it is page 3D38-0261 for the English. As I said, 3D38-0261 and 62, or 0263 as well. Now, could you focus on the date, please, of that first document. It's in the upper right-hand corner, and it says that it is about a transit shipment for BiH. The date of the document is as you can see. So all these three documents are tied into one. They are linked together and refer to just one event.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, following the Judge's guide-lines, I'll try and be as brief as possible. Sometimes it's difficult, but, anyway, I'll do my best. 4.700.000 kilograms of diesel fuel for Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived in just this one tanker. It was just one shipment, and it went towards Sarajevo and to the population, of course, and probably some companies, but to the BH Army. It went to Bosnia-Herzegovina through the port of Ploce. It was allowed free passage through the HVO check-points and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And you have the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The shipment came from the USSR, is that right, for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 17th of August, 1993, is the date. From the 14th to the 17th, depending on the bill of lading, loading, unloading, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now 3D32-1282 is the next document I'd like us to look at. Or, rather, that's the 17th, 0263, and that's the entry -- the entry papers.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was continuous. The same happened in September and especially just before the winter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's right, but we wanted to point this out because we were speaking in general terms, without showing an actual document. So that's why I wanted to show this. Now, General, I have marked the page numbers in the book or the binder so that you'll be able to find your way more easily, because some pages are not very legible in Croatian, the copies. The next annex that I'd like us to look at is the care of the wounded BiH soldiers and civilians, mostly Bosniaks, Muslims, in the hospitals of the 7 Republic of Croatia in 1992 and 1995. And the file begins on page 3D32-1306, 8 and in English it is on page 3D38-0289. And we have a total of 1.180 documents that the Defence team has managed to collect, and 59 are in the files or the annex. And that has a separate number, but we're not going to deal with that now. Anyway, may we have your comments on 3D32-1307, which is the map. 3D38-0292. And I'm making pauses because of the transcript, to help the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from these documents and looking at the documents, I know this, of course, all firsthand, because my department in the Defence Ministry was involved in this, the transport and so on, so I was fully versed with what was going on in HZ-HB, and what the Defence Department was doing, and what Petkovic was doing, and so on and so forth. But these are not all the places. These are just some of the places where these people were treated; the most important ones, of course. Split, there was Firule, Krizine, Toplice, and then there was Zagreb. And when I say "Zagreb," I mean ten hospitals, not just one hospital in Zagreb, but ten hospitals, Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci, Metkovici, there was -- Metkovic there was a large hospital there for what in military terms would have been a separate echelon, second echelon: Then in Varazdin, there were the Varazdin "sketoplice" [phoen], spa areas, and so on. So if you're going to show some other documents, then we might see all those other places there too. And I know that over 10.000 people who were listed here were treated in Croatia. They were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, received treatment. And based on my information, most of them were Muslims. And from my own experience, I know, especially in 1993, when I left and went in 1994 and 1995, as my own personal involvement, I selected the military hospital in Zagreb to focus on, and I paid regular visits there to the wounded from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were both Croats and Muslims, and I visited them, especially at the orthopaedics ward, because I knew Dr. Reljica very well and I helped him write two books. One on -- one orthopaedic method of bone joining, and so on and so forth. But, anyway, I would always take 10 or 20 kilos of cigarettes. I would receive those cigarettes or I would purchase them, and through my own personal collections and some enterprises, I was able to procure for this special orthopaedic procedure some of the parts they needed, the surgical parts like the wires, and bolts, and so on. So on one occasion, this amounted to 20.000 German marks, and another occasion 30.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you something with respect to these two maps here at the beginning of this annex or file. How were they compiled? How were they drawn up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were drawn up on the basis of the information and facts that I received or, rather, which the team received on the basis of a request tabled here, and we sent this out to the Association of Croatian Physicians Volunteers, 1991. And on the basis of the information we received from the hospitals or, rather, this association, we were able to draw up these maps. So the maps were drawn up on the basis of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I'd just like to say that the document that the general referred to, and relates to providing 8 information from the Association of Croatian Volunteer Physicians, 1990-1991, is to be found on 3D32-1309 for the Croatian version and 3D38-0292.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, a while ago we had the map in front of us on the screen, and we can see that there were eight hospitals that were admitting wounded people. On this document, I see that you have indicated that these injured people could be civilians and soldiers from the ABiH, and you have written down here "3D38-0290." So my question is a very accurate question. Let's take the case of an ABiH soldier that is wounded, who is being carried to a hospital, one of the hospitals in Split. This injured person will be cared for, operated on, and so on and so forth. As far as you know, when he is in this hospital, is he considered to be a prisoner of war? In other words, he is being monitored 24 hours a day? Or he is admitted into the hospital with the influx of other people who have been wounded, i.e., soldiers and civilians, and everybody is in there together, and once he is cured and is better, he is told he can leave? How did things happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely as you've just stated. There was no difference, no difference at all between the wounded of any ethnic community. There were no controls. Once the treatment was completed, that person was free to go back or to go wherever they wanted, and they didn't pay for their treatment at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I'm putting this question to you because this was part of an international armed conflict. As far as you know, when there is a conflict and when you are in conflict with your opponent, and when the soldiers of the opposite side are taken prisoner, when these people are being cared for, are they being monitored or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, based on what I learned reading books and -- the wounded from the enemy side are placed in separate wards, and they are under guard, considered as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: You said a moment ago -- I'm a little bit surprised by this, but if you say so, you must be relying on tangible material. You said that they were cared for and they were free to go back to their respective units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I marked pages in your book that I would like us to go to so as to save some time, in the print-out, not the one in e-court but to the left-hand side. Yes. And now I suggest that we go to page 3D32-1325. I also marked the page numbers on your copy. The English version is 3D38-0308. The date of the document is the 9th of November, 1992. It says here "Assistant Commander For Logistics, Edin Batlak. It says here Effendi Adem Smajic, who is in Rijeka. What can you tell us about this document, and what does this document show as regards the way and the problems regarding the supply and delivery of humanitarian aid, medications, and other necessary items?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows here -- we're talking about 7 tonnes of medications, medicines, and the date is the 9th of November in 1992. There's always one thing at stake here. Combat operations are the only thing, and these are operations against the Army of Republika Srpska. It was only the combat operations that could postpone or disrupt for a period of time the passage of convoys. So it was not done because of some attitudes or intentions, because on the Croatian side this was done -- well, Croatia treated Bosnia-Herzegovina the same way it treated itself. There was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the record and for the Chamber's benefit, Rijeka is where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We will skip 1992, as instructed by the Trial Chamber. Could you please go to 3D32-1340. The English version is 3D38-0323. This document is shown here, and we will discuss it only to get the full picture. But I have to tell the Chamber, and also for the record, that this is an exhibit, 2D00321. So that's the number of the exhibit. It is a document dated the 8th of June, 1993. Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. It is signed by Colonel Dr. Tugomir Gveric. Did you know Dr. Gveric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please go to the next page. It's 3D32-1342 or 3D38-0324. That's the English version. The document is dated the 16th of May, 1993. It's again a consignment destined for the BH Army. Again, it's signed by Dr. Gveric. And this wraps up the chapter about the provision of medical aid to Mostar. And could you please now provide a more detailed answer to His Honour Judge Antonetti's question, if you look at 3D32-1343, the English is 3D38-0325.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what I knew during the war and what I know now, this is what I can say: The number of wounded soldiers and civilians, who were predominantly of Muslim ethnicity, with names -- well, based on the information that I was able to gather, and this is probably not the full data, the number is 10.623 people. Those people were injured in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were transferred through the -- what was called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this was a huge job. Think about the number of cars that had to head towards Split or to Slavonski Brod, northwards. So it's easy to calculate all those who were in the authorities took part in it, and in particular it was the Medical Corps and the Defence Department and the Main Staff. They -- we had to do most of the work, in terms of organisation; how many times cars had to leave with the wounded or sick people, the helicopters had to take off to evacuate them, how much money it cost. But I state with full responsibility that the data are correct and there was no distinction made on any basis, and all those people were treated free of charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like to point your attention to 3D38-1354, or 3D38-0331, that's the English version. This is the document dated the 17th of June, 1998. The director of the Split Hospital, Dr. Biocic, issued this document, and here we get some information about the number of people treated in the hospitals in Split.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the record and for the Trial Chamber's benefit, this piece of information was provided to the Office for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, so that this is an authentic document. And before that, we have lists of persons treated, and we've already shown it in court, and there is no need for us to go back to those lists one by one, unless of course you think that you would like to say something about that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have anything to add, apart from the fact that there is a map attached here indicating how many and from what locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- how much aid was sent from Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please give us the number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 3D32-1308, and I don't know the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, I'll provide the English reference. Let me just find it. It's 3D38-0291.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can see that in terms of sending the aid, there is no Herceg-Bosna, there is no Banovina. The medicines went to a greater extent to the Muslim people and the BH Army than to the HVO. So, Ms. Pinter, 1356, the 1995 note of gratitude from Alija Izetbegovic to the hospital in Firule.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, that was the next document in line after the memo from the Office for Cooperation. Do you know anything about the circumstances under which this note of gratitude was sent? Why was this note of appreciation sent? Oh, I'm sorry, the number is 3D32-1356, and the English version is 3D38-0336. Did you know how Ejub Ganic was hurt?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was saved in an urgent intervention, and after so much good was done somebody finally thought of actually thanking the hospital, Dr. Biocic and his team, and the head nurse in particular, because throughout the war -- well, the document speaks for itself. Well, I don't have to explain now that at one point those people realised what -- or had they realised what friend they had in Croatia, well, they would never have launched the aggression on us. There would never have been this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in this book we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt. This letter is dated 9 July 1995. That is rather after the facts here. It does not give any indication as to at what time Dr. Ganic had had his car accident. It is also, of course, not said whether there was any relation between the car accident and the war. Mr. Praljak, do you know when that accident took place, when this aid was extended to Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, well, the accident happened in 1995, before the 9th of July. I don't know the exact date. But, please, the sentence reads as follows: "As many times before, your experts --" or, rather, "your expert work and dedication to the humanitarian vocation of a physician provided results at the time when this was really urgent, and this will not be forgotten here." So it says here "as many times before." This sentence tells you that Mr. Izetbegovic was very much aware of all those things that I was talking about, what happened before 1995; in other words, in 1993 and 1994, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, as regards this aid, we have this note of appreciation to the Split Hospital and to the Split Caritas. Would you like us to go through them one by one and to comment on them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If they are admitted into evidence, they will show how much aid went to what locations, and this will confirm the veracity of the map that I drew.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Documents are at pages 3D32-1361. The English version is 3D38 -0341; 3D32-1362, 3D38-0342, that's it's English. And now we move to the next file entitled "The Refugees and Displaced Persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia." It begins at page 3D32-1363. The English version begins at 3D38-0344. And the file contains 511 documents -- or, rather, that's the total number of documents, and the file contains 72 documents. The first document in the file has already been dealt with in the course of your testimony the first week, and we will not be going into that. Could you please go to the document at page 3D32-1365. The English version does not exist because this is a document that is written in both languages, English and Croatian. The date is the 26th of November, 1992. It's an estimate of the number of inhabitants and displaced persons, provided by the UNICEF, and I would like to draw your attention and ask you how much you know about that, how much you know about the data listed in item 6, 7, and 8 of this document. It's the ethnic structure of the inhabitants, the age of the children, and the nationality of the displaced persons. And as I've already told you, it's the 26th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Adalbert Rebic testified here before me, and he is an expert, much more so than I am. This document pertains only to Split. This is the UNICEF office in Split. And it tells you where they had come from; Prijedor, Kljuc. And then you have the age, the ethnicity. There is 31.862 Muslims, 26.000 Croats, and 7.000 Serbs, 7.700 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no refugee --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I wanted you to look at the stamp at the bottom of this document. It was issued by the Territorial Defence in Travnik, the Municipal Civilian Protection Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So it's a document they issued, listing the places of origin of the displaced persons, and this breakdown according to those categories. What we are interested in is Travnik and Jajce.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's after the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Document 3D32-1367, the English version is 3D38-0347, just for the record, is already an exhibit under 1D01269. This is a letter dated 4 November 1993. Franjo Kumarica. Who is Franjo Kumarica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Kumarica is a bishop, he's the bishop of Banja Luka. Bosnia-Herzegovina is divided into three bishopries. One of them is the bishopry of Banja Luka, and he is the bishop of Banja Luka. He has been there all the time, despite all the obstacles. He was even a candidate for the Nobel Peace Prize as a result of his activities. Here it says what's happening to the refugees from Vares, once Vares had fallen. And he writes to Mr. Prlic here, asking him what would happen with those people, 90 percent Croats and 10 percent Serbs. And he appeals to the government, asking the government to accommodate all those people. And he's talking about anything between 5.000 and 10.000 people, although there were more of them even. He is looking for and asking for oil, buses, and so on and so forth. To put it simply, those people at that time were nothing but a collateral victim of the conflict. They could not remain in the area where their army had lost the war. They were afraid of a retaliation, and they are in the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Franjo Kumarica is asking for help to move them towards the HZ-HB territory in any way, which means that he needed oil and buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you now open 3D32-1370, and in the English it is 3D38-0350. The date is 19 April 1994. It is still within the framework of the indictment. The letter is dated to the UNHCR and sent by the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the subject is moving Bosniaks to the third countries. Were you aware of this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What can we conclude, based on the content of this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a programme that was not very clear to me, to be honest. I don't know what were the political reasons that made the UNHCR act subversively and displace as many people as possible to the third countries. The whole strategy in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with regard to the refugees and displaced persons, was -- and I myself worked with a group of sociologists in my department. We were working on a study with this regard, based on the facts which we were aware of and which were learned about from documents of the United Nations. Refugees who move far away from their place of origin hardly ever go back to that place of origin. Ten or 15 percent a year will never go back to their place of origin, which means that the full rate is 10 to 15 percent every subsequent year. And that's why an attempt should have been made to displace people as close to their place of origin, to help them believe that they will once return. The UNHCR resettled them far away. Bisera Turkovic objected to that, but I can't speak about their motives because I'm not clear to this very day what those were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would like to draw attention to the first paragraph, where it says that the UNHCR staff rallies the refugees, telling them that they cannot safely return to Mostar. They say that Mostar is not safe either for the Croats or the Serbs, let alone for the Muslims, as they highlight. They say that the Muslims are not allowed to enter Mostar, let alone live there, and that they should be patient and do not embark on the convoys allegedly prepared for their return. However, the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not agree with such activities on the part of the UNHCR, and they want an explanation as to why they're acting contrary to their mandate. That's why the document is important, because it shows that displacing Bosniaks from the territory of -- from the territory of Croatia was not due to the actions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to what I think is a leading question or a statement or comment on the evidence by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please avoid leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can, I believe. It says so in the document, and, Ms. Pinter, this is not only about Mostar. Mostar is given just by way of example. However, this was also done in Gasinci, Savudrija, Ucka, Varazdin, Obonjan. And it says here that there is a feeling of instability and panic amongst the refugees. The activities of the UNHCR are absolutely puzzling. Resettlement from Croatia and preventing people from possibly going back home was done to the activities of the UNHCR for logically unknown reasons. There must be some kind of logic behind all that, but, in any case, that logic was neither correct, nor honest, nor fair. I don't know what this is all about. I can only explain all that by some political games which I can't say anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document, which comes from the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact there are two points that the embassy is emphasizing. The first is in the first paragraph of this document. The document states that in Mostar, security is not provided for, both for Croats -- neither for the Croats, nor for the Serbs, nor for the Muslims, says the text. We are referring here to a period of April 1994, but apparently since there was no security provided in Mostar at the time, that explains why it was difficult to bring back the Muslims. Do you agree with the statement that is made here by the embassy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, it is not the embassy that says that the return in Mostar is not safe. It is the UNHCR that claims that the return to Mostar is not safe. This is at the time when the conflicts had stopped, and Mostar was as safe as any other place. It may have happened that the Army of Republika Srpska - but that was rare at the time - fired a shell. But Mostar was safe enough to start embarking on an organised return of all those who had left Mostar. The embassy does not agree with the estimate provided by the UNHCR, which has not been provided only for Mostar, but for some other places. This means that the UNHCR spread panic and lies. Let us be clear on that. The UNHCR lied to the refugees when they told them that they would lose their status in Croatia, which was not true. The status of refugee in Croatia could be lost only if the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., its organs, signed the document to the effect that the refugee could be returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina and that where he was returning to was safe. It was only then that the Republic of Croatia could abolish the status of refugee, when this was confirmed by the state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Otherwise, they could not have lost the status of refugees. And this was never done for any refugee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, you have anticipated on the question I wanted to do ask you about the second paragraph. According to this embassy, the UNHCR notes that the Republic of Croatia wants to abolish this status of refugee and that Croatia would like to organise convoys to other countries, in particular for Muslims. Of course, this could be related to the criminal enterprise, but we are talking here about April 1994. To your knowledge, at that point in time was this the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you misunderstood me, or maybe it's down to the interpretation. First of all, the conflict had already ended. Second of all, the UNHCR promised the refugees and said, In the Republic of Croatia, which is not true, not correct, the republic, If Croatia abolishes your status of refugee, then the UNHCR would organise convoys for third countries. And if anybody is talking about ethnic cleansing and the joint criminal enterprise, then to the least extent, at least it would apply to the UNHCR, not Croatia, because it was the UNHCR that spread lies. It spoke "pro futuro" about something that did not exist, and they said to the refugees, You can lose your refugee status. It would be better for you to sit on convoys and let us take you somewhere else. It is not Croatia that organised convoys. It was, rather, the UNHCR that organised those convoys to take the refugees to third countries, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, why would the UNHCR play such a game?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could speculate, based on some foundations that I can't prove. It was simply an attempt to blacken the country. All sorts of games, spy games, counter-spy games, intelligence games were played at all levels by all countries and blocks. All that was going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To follow up on this document, let's look at 3D32-1372, and in the English it's 3D38-0352. This is another letter by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the Office of Refugees and Displaced Persons, on the same date, on the 19th of April, 1994. General, are you familiar with the document? Can you say something about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, we have already seen this document. I believe that it already has a number. I remember having seen it before this Trial Chamber already, and it testifies once again that the UNHCR is asking from Croatia to introduce some order into the organisation that deals with the accommodation of civilians from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it says that the proposals to that effect will be given by Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document speaks about the UNHCR. The UNHCR is an organisation that behaves the way it did, and people behaved over there as if they had come to a Papau state. I don't want to offend anybody. Everybody showed very imperialistic behavior. At the very beginning of this trial, I misused the word "French impressionist" for "French imperialist." However, there was a lot of those who walked around Bosnia-Herzegovina who behaved as imperialists. That's what I call them. They came with no respect for anybody. I'm not saying that all of them were like that, but a lot of them did not show any respect for the state, for the rules of behavior. Why was that the case? I will leave it to the Trial Chamber to draw their own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Office for Refugees and DPs, did they also cooperate with the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the matters, as far as I know, in absolutely every single matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. That document was indeed shown in the courtroom, but has not been admitted. That's why I produced it now, and it was offered as 3D00304. I have been instructed by Ms. Nozica that on page 23, line 13, there is a mistake; that the UNHCR is asking from Croatia to install some order into the organisation of the accommodation of civilians from Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as I know and as far as I remember, this was not the UNHCR who requested that. It was requested by --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was requested by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this letter, if we look at the first paragraph, this is dated the 19th of April, 1994. Dates are important. It seems, according to the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there is a situation that is due to the arrival of a number of refugees at the borders of the Republic of Croatia. According to the embassy, these people would like to go to a third country, but it seems that a criticism has been levelled at them by the UNHCR, because the embassy says "with the help of the UNHCR." How can you decipher this letter? One could read it several ways, couldn't one? How do you interpret this? Is this a call for help on the part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is sent to the Republic of Croatia to put an end to the situation? Or is it just realising that this is a situation which nobody can control, since it is the end of the conflict, and that they feel that their future lies in third countries and not in Bosnia-Herzegovina? As far as you know at the time in the month of April 1994, how many refugees were arriving at the borders every day? That said, there was no fighting anymore at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to how many refugees came to the borders, I wouldn't be able to answer that. I don't have that answer. I would refrain from offering any answer to that effect. However, I would not refrain from answering the next question. The Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina was aware of all that I have just said; that if you want the refugees to return to their place of origin, they have to be as close as possible, but they have to be safe, of course, but the point being they have to be close to the place from which they had fled. Your Honours, you will understand why this was being done if you look at the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. 200.000 Croats have never returned to the Republika Srpska. Over 200.000 Muslims have never returned there, to Republika Srpska. As for the eastern part of Bosnia, Vares, Jajce, a lot of Croats have never returned there. The largest number of refugees into the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are there where the territory was under the control of the HVO. The data to that effect exists. I can submit all that to you. In my view, there was some sort of a political game to move those people as far from the country as possible. And from my Defence team you can request and receive the number of Bosniaks who live in the USA, the Netherlands, Sweden, the Kingdom of Norway, who already have children, second generation, who are unlikely to ever return to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer was a very lengthy one. You could have made it shorter. This leads to another question which you have raised, but you didn't realise it when you were saying it. You said that 200.000 Muslims never returned to the Republika Srpska, so whilst I was listening to you I was going back in time a little bit and going back to April 1994, the beginning of 1994, and then the second half of 1993, when a Muslim came to the frontier or the border of the Republic of Croatia with the help of UNHCR and perhaps even with a certificate from Sweden, for instance, some paper that would let him pass the frontier. How can you establish a distinction between the Muslim who leaves Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the presence of Serbs or because of the presence of the HVO? How can you make the distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, a correction. More than 200.000 Croats from Republika Srpska and far more than 200.000 Muslims from Republika Srpska never returned to this day. That's the first point. Secondly, as far as Croatia is concerned, no differentiation was made between people, where they had come from and why. We didn't ask that question. That's the first point. And, number two, they were first accommodated in one of the centres in Croatia, and then they -- we had these emissaries who started saying, Well, the UNHCR said it would be better for you to leave. You won't be able to go back because there's shooting over there. Of course, some people wanted to leave. That's also true. But, anyway, the UNHCR and the various emissaries tried to have as many refugees as possible re-leave the Republic of Croatia. Of course, Croatia could do nothing. If some of them wanted to leave and somebody was willing to take them in, it couldn't do anything. But Bosnia-Herzegovina complained, because these people were quite conscious of the fact that the further they went and the longer they stayed there, that the likelihood of them returning was slim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I recognise this may be an issue for cross-examination, but we're talking about April of 1994, and I think it bears wondering whether what -- what the general status was in Croatia at the time and how it is that he knows what UNHCR or purports to know what UNHCR was doing at the time and what its policies were. How was he even involved in any of these issues? I can save that for later, but it's going to be quite a long time. It seemed worth noting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. On several occasions you have mentioned the UNHCR, the policies of the UNHCR, but do you have anything tangible to rely on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the return at the beginning of November -- or, rather, after I returned from Bosnia-Herzegovina in November, I was the porte-parole, the spokesman for the Ministry of Defence, which means that I had all the information at my disposal. I was also a military adviser to President Tudjman, and I was well versed in everything that was going on in the country. I was a well-informed person by virtue of the office I held and also because I knew lots of people. But, anyway, information would come to us. Information would be placed on my table from all over, from the SIS, the Internal Affairs Ministry, and so on, as to what was going on in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could round off the topic. General, could you turn to 3D32-1-113, and the English is 3D38-0392. It's a graphic spread of refugees and displaced persons in Croatia from 1992, 1993, 1994 -- or, rather, 1995. And since Judge Antonetti asked you about 1994 and the document we were discussing was 1994 with respect to the number of refugees and displaced persons, can you comment on this graph or diagram? 3D32-1-113 is the number of the Croatian version. I can hand it to you. We have a schematic here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean "1-11"?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Or I might be reading it out wrongly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 1413 is the number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, that's better.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm a bit short-sighted, so it looked like a "4," but anyway --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's on the screen in colour. Perhaps that will be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything is clear now. That is information for 1992, '3, '4 and '5, the figures there, and that's it. It's a diagram showing how many refugees and displaced persons there were in Croatia in these different years, and there's nothing to add or subtract there. There, it's the correct information. I think that this is UNHCR data.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, fine. I'd like to go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do not find this informative, I must say. The legends are only in Croatian, and I do not see what it means. Could it be explained a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D38-0392 will give you the English, the English description of the legend on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The green is refugees, and the blue are the displaced persons. I'd just like to add that people -- there was -- there were comings and goings, of course, but this is a constant number. It's not the total number of refugees and displaced persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia. People went further on to Hungary, and many of them went further on still to Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, would you turn to page 3D32-1379. The document's already an exhibit, and it's 5D00064. But you mentioned several times a joint statement given by Dr. Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic of the 15th of June 1992. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English you want? Yes, I'm just about to give the number. It is 3D38-0358.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can you tell me why the statements were signed in Zagreb and Sarajevo on the 15th of June? Do you have any information about that, and what can you tell us about this joint statement? What do you know about it and the circumstances under which it was given, and what were the consequences of that statement and its signing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not crystal -- well, it's a crystal-clear joint statement, so I don't think there's anything to add, in general terms, unless you want to know something specific. It's very clear as it stands. Now, you asked me why in Zagreb and Sarajevo. Because up until that date, Mr. Izetbegovic was not able to leave Sarajevo, and I think that that is mentioned somewhere in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that Mr. Izetbegovic cannot leave Sarajevo, and then the two presidents, President Franjo Tudjman and the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, agreed to write a joint statement of this kind, which is quite clear; it's clear cut. So unless you have any specific question, I don't think there's any need for me to comment. It reads and says what it says. The important point is that in point 1, it says taking into consideration the fact that the Republic of Croatia has recognised the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has recognised the Republic of Croatia, both presidents hereby state that immediate steps need to be taken in order for diplomatic relations to be established at embassy level. And then it goes on to mention refugees. Well, if you want me to comment, that would take us too far.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I just wanted you to explain why Sarajevo and Zagreb. It is now -- is it time for the break, or are we going to go on for 10 or 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not time for the break yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, fine. So let's move to the next file, which relates to the ex-territorial education of pupils from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nika, you have the 8th of July, this joint statement signed, because Mr. Izetbegovic did, in fact, manage to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. So immediately upon his arrival in Zagreb on the 8th of July, they signed an almost identical statement. And point 2 is particularly important there, and it is 3D32-1377. That's the number, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The English version is 3D38-0357 and 0358, because it takes up two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as far as item 3 of this joint statement is concerned, it relates to the two armies, the HVO and the ABiH. This document is signed by Izetbegovic and Tudjman. Therefore, one has reason to believe that when Mr. Izetbegovic signs this document, he knows what he is signing. In paragraph 3, it says as follows: that the Republic of Croatia is also supporting the efforts of the Presidency of Bosnia to consolidate the republic by integrating all the armies or all the armed components in a unified army placed under the command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This document seems to be saying that there are two armies, in fact, and Izetbegovic admits to this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in continuation of my testimony, I will be showing, using different sources, how Mr. Izetbegovic behaved, in actual fact, and why the HZ-HB and HVO had to be established. We were the regular army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in that respect --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, Judge Antonetti is referring to a document, not the one we've just looked at.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's referring to June. Yes, June, and Croatia asked that the components be united, that is to say, that the governments, the two governments, meet and that a joint command be found. I will prove later on that part of the BH Army Command, especially Sefer Halilovic, and parts of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina who controlled Alija Izetbegovic, that nothing could be done with them. Our efforts were futile. We -- our efforts were enormous, on a daily basis, but they did not bear fruit, and you will be able to see why they did not bear fruit. I will show why they did not bear fruit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, General. Now I'd like us to go back to the joint statement dated the 8th of July. And could you focus on point 5, which is the last point of that joint statement which was signed in Helsinki. So look at point 5. That's what I'm interested in, especially with respect to the internal setup of the state. You've already talked about this, but once again could you explain to the Court what the substance of the negotiations were and what the positions taken by the Republic of Croatia were and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to the internal system of BH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A, Croatia is a state. B, Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state. C, the HVO is the regular army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. D, we wish, as a constituent peoples, to take part in agreement about the internal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One man/one vote is unitarianism. That was unacceptable. Our joint enemy was the one that attacked us; that is to say, the Army of Republika Srpska was our joint enemy, and the Yugoslav People's Army. And, E, Mr. Izetbegovic -- well, I had a meeting with him, but never, ever did he say how he saw the internal setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All he did was to refuse -- he would refuse the various proposals, but never -- and said what he didn't want, but he never said what he did want and never made a proposal for the building up of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina. He never laid down a platform for the kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina he wanted to see so that we could work jointly. And if something was agreed with the international community, he would override it, he would go and create complete chaos. And I'll come to that in due course, but I don't think this is the right time to go into those matters now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I suggest we move on to another area. We'll skip the question of refugees in 1992, because I think that we have already dealt with the topic extensively in our discussions so far. So please turn now to page 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Since you are addressing another topic, maybe it would be the right time to have a break. We should have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have some administrative matters. I believe you have some matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Pursuant to your oral decision earlier this afternoon, Your Honour, I have an IC number to give to the latest list of documents submitted by the Praljak Defence for the list up until today that they intend to submit through the witness. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1010. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I'd like to go into closed session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to redact lines 6, 7, and 8 of what was just stated. We shall continue the examination. General Praljak, I have a question, a follow-up question. A moment ago, we saw tables for 1992, 1993, 1994, and these tables had two colours, those who were expelled and for refugees. Now, during the break I was thinking about the table for 1995. At that time, there was no longer a conflict, people were not shooting at each other. Why is it, as I look at this table, that you can see that the number increases as the months go by? Can you give us an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was fierce fighting in those years, but after the Washington Agreements there were no conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO, but the Republika Srpska Army continued its work all the way up to the Dayton Accords, or, rather, up until the time when in Operation Storm the Croatian Army, the BH Army, and the HVO managed to achieve some military success. So the war did not end in Eastern Bosnia, it was still going on, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In other words, your answer here completes what you said before the break; in other words, there are a number of Muslim refugees whose fate is directly linked to the Serbs as regards the year 1995. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, as we've said before the break, we'll move on to the next file. That's the ex-territorial education of the students from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. It begins at page 3D32-1415. The English is 3D38-0394. The total number of files that the Defence has is 67. The file contains 30 of those. Could we please get the chart showing how many ex-territorial schools there were, so could you please open 3D32-1416 or, English, 3D38-0395. And if you could please comment on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, in those schools -- well, they were not attended by Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those schools were made solely for the students from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were Bosniaks to attend if they wished so, their own classes, so that they could be taught the history of their own country, the literature of their country, and I've already gone through all this with another witness at this trial. So in the schools that are shown on this map, classes were organised from Bosniak pupils, Bosniak students, where they were taught language, literature, and history. That was the first time that the term "Bosniak language" was used. It was not in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to some constitutional provision. It was used for the first time in Croatia, because it was recognised as a right of a people to use their own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps just one more document from this file. That would be the number of students from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. The document is at page 32-1425, and in English it's 3D38-0405. The document was issued by the minister of education and culture, and it's a report to the Government of the Republic of Croatia, the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees. Is there anything in particular that you would like to draw our attention to? Perhaps the number of students, the period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it says here that the greatest number of students from Bosnia and Herzegovina voluntarily and at their own request participated in the education system of the Republic of Croatia, but some of those students, Bosniaks naturally, because Croats did not have any need to have any special curricula, some of those students wanted to have ex-territorial education and were given what they wanted. Of course, efforts were made for the teachers who taught language, culture, and history to be from Bosnia and Herzegovina, if there were any. So it is a separate segment of the education, of the schooling system in the Republic of Croatia, organised for the children of the refugees, Muslim refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the Croatian budget had some funds earmarked for those schools. I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Perhaps only to say that this memo refers to the school year 1993-1994, because this is our reverential period and the number of students who attended those classes. To save some time and to move on to some other topics, because we have a lot of things to cover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would still like to ask a question, Mr. Praljak. What do we have to imagine with these special schools? One possibility is that there was a special building which says "School for Bosniaks," something like that, where the schooling was done for these students. And the other possibility is that within the normal schools, there was a special curriculum where language, literature, and history were taught in separate special classes for the Bosniak students. Was it the latter, or the former, or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both options, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. In some areas, there were just regular schools where language, culture and history were taught separately, in separate classes, and in areas where there was a large refugee campus, then classes were organised separately; perhaps not in a separate school building, but there was a building that was used for that purpose. And if I can give you a more extended explanation, in 1993 there were some problems on the islands because people wanted to have tourists and then they wanted the schools -- the classes to move out of some of the buildings that they wanted to use for the tourist trade, so people made due in all kinds of ways. So, for instance, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let us move on to our next topic, the next file. That's the aid of the Republic of Croatia to the Bihac enclave in the course of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence has 1.790 documents, and 113 documents are used in the file. It begins at 3D32-1446.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version is 3D38-0431.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could give us some general comments about this aid, and then we will deal with one of the documents in detail.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as briefly as possible, in some parts of the overall aid that Republic of Croatia provided to Bihac, I, myself, participated; for instance, in the transfer of some units, using the route that was still open, that went through the Serb lines, so to speak. And I can say that from 1992 until the operation that was launched in order to prevent the fall of Bihac, and it was in the offing, it was to suffer the same fate as Srebrenica, then the Croatian Army got the green light from the international community, from the Americans, to launch an operation together with the HVO and the BH Army, to launch an offensive and to liberate Bihac, and then we came -- we reached Banja Luka. And then we were stopped. That was again a decision by the Americans. Throughout that period, the overall assistance that was provided to the Bihac area went through Croatia by air, aeroplanes, helicopters. Some aid got in through the lines, and had it not been the case, had the Croatian Army not intervened, Bihac would have suffered the same fate as Srebrenica, and it would not have been able to survive without the assistance of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, to get a time-frame, when was this joint operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The joint operation was launched in early autumn 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We've talked about the aid -- yes, I am being warned that I'm speaking too fast. We spoke about the retraining for aeroplanes. Could we please move to page 3D32-1485. The English version is 3D38-0477. This was signed by the chief of the system. Well, I can't read it because it's -- at any rate, it's Sefer Halilovic, the Supreme Command Staff of the BH Army, Sarajevo, issuing an order to retrain the pilots. You talked about that, but this document shows clearly who those pilots were, what period, what number of persons was covered, and what aeroplanes. Perhaps you could comment on that. Why was this retraining important? How was it possible to reach the enclave of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mostly used the Antonov aircraft. Let me not describe how lights were switched on and off and how there had to be silence on board the aircraft. The pilots provided statements for this Tribunal and described all that in very minor detail. I repeat, everything, every single thing in the over 1.000 documents, and I know it is impossible to go through all of them, the Trial Chamber would be too busy doing that, but when I say "everything, every single thing," I mean everything; food, weapons, the transport of the wounded, the training of the pilots, and the units that were infiltrating everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have already introduced documents that concern the assistance of that kind, and now I propose that we should move to the last file in the binder. And the file concerns the assistance of the Republic of Croatia in the area of sport in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is on page 3D32-1560, and in the English it is 3D38-0577. We have a total of three documents, and all three are in the file. However, you have some personal knowledge about this type of assistance on the part of the Republic of Croatia. I would kindly ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what you know about all that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I was partly informed at the time. The president of the Croatian Olympic Committee, Anto Vrdoljak, and the current permanent member of the International Olympic Committee, a film director as well, a very well-known Croatian film director whom I've known for decades, he was the vice-president of the Presidency of Croatia after the first democratic elections. So he was the one who stood in for Franjo Tudjman if that was necessary. He was a member of the VONS, he was the general manager of the Croatian TV during those hard times, and so on and so forth. He was -- or, rather, due to his good connections with Mr. Samaranch, Juan Samaranch, the Croatian athletes managed to get an invitation to Barcelona in 1992. And together with them, on board the same aircraft, there were also the athletes of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the athletes of Bosnia and Herzegovina who travelled at the expense of the Croatian state. They had been prepared somewhere in Istria, in Ravan perhaps; that was also at the expense of the Croatian state. And they flew on board the same airline by the Croatian airline company because Vrdoljak was also a member of the supervisory board of that airline company. So a high state official assisted in the organisation of all that. I claim that this is very important because of the fact that if there had been a desire to break up a state, to carve it up, and to take a part of it as its own, it would certainly not have been help to appear at such big sporting events. And I also remember that there was a big issue of the money. It cost 2 million German marks to do all that, and I know that the ministers of finance complained about the amount of money, which was huge for Croatia at the time. But Franjo Tudjman was adamant and he said, Give us the money. We are sending both delegations to Barcelona, because that is very important. And that's how Bosnia-Herzegovina appeared, under its own flags featuring lilies. The second document also concerns the same thing. However, the year is 1993, and in France the Mediterranean Games took place there, and the story goes the same. Croatia took the delegation of Bosnian athletes under its wing. They travelled together on the same aircraft. They had been in training in Istria, where there was peace. They could not have trained in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And again the issue may be erased, what happened in 1993. By doing that, Croatia stated very clearly that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a Mediterranean state. It only has one very short stretch of the coast, a line of some 10 or 12 kilometres. If there had been a plan in place to take Neum in Herzegovina or cut it off from the sea, then obviously they would not have taken a delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to a sporting event where it was confirmed that it was a Mediterranean state rather than a landlocked state. Tonci Vrdoljak or, rather, Anto Vrdoljak issued a statement to that effect, and he described all that. And if the Trial Chamber wishes to read this, they can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please give us the date of the Mediterranean Games? This is very important and very indicative. You'll find this at the very beginning of the document, if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mediterranean Games took place between the 10th June and 27th June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Year?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the document is on page 3D32-1562, or in the English version it is 3D38-0579. And I believe that we can now talk about the basketball team.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't have to. What I want to say is that a similar cooperation existed in the area of culture, theatre, the written word, and so on forth. Many writers and actors at the time had fled from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they acted in Croatian shows, they appeared in Croatian TV, films, and I know that first-hand. I'm sharing this with you as reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Okay. We can then close this big binder, and we're moving on to a different topic. I have to provide an explanation to the Trial Chamber. Since when we were talking about the books last week and there were problems in following the books on e-court, we have scanned all the books again, and I'm going to refer you to their new numbers in order to avoid any problems in following the documents on e-court. There may be a little problem at the outset until we are in sync. The books we are going to discuss now are in the binder number 2 and also in binder number 3 that we provided to everybody last week. However, I would kindly ask the usher, because before the beginning of this session we submitted Mohammed Filipovic's book, "I Was Alija's Diplomat," which has been rescanned and is now 3D03554. And also under number 3D03557, this is the second part of that book. At the beginning of this session, I provided four copies for the Trial Chamber. These two, I'm going to show them to you, this is what they looked like. The general has his own copy. I've already mentioned the name. General, you prepared a few books that you want to discuss and that you find very significant, and you find their contents important for the understanding of the circumstances that surrounded all of the events. At the beginning, I would like to ask you who Muhamed Filipovic was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared the books, Your Honours, because it is much better if the Muslims and Bosniaks, who have written about the war and the events that we are discussing here now, provide information and claims, because their claims and the information they provide show that they agree with my own claims, what I am stating here. Obviously, there is always a danger, and the danger is very realistic, that an accused for war crimes is less credible or believed than somebody else. That's why I wanted to show you what a Muslim author knows and writes about the same things that I've spoken about. I've prepared some books by high officials, generals of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who are all Muslims. Mr. Filipovic is a participant in the parties in war. He was a partisan from the year 1943. He was a student first in Belgrade and later on in Zagreb. He was a student of philosophy there. He returned to Sarajevo, where he obtained his PhD, and he was a faculty member of the School of Philosophy in Sarajevo, where he taught ontology and logic or ethnics. He has authored some 10 or 11 books, which most of them deal with the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the history of Muslim or Bosniak people. He's also a member of the Academia of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has been a member since the 1970s of the last century, and he's one of the most prominent intellectuals among the ranks of the Muslim Bosniak people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the end of the war, he was a diplomat, he participated in the negotiations in Geneva, and he was also a prominent member of the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And together with Mr. Zulfikarpasic, he was the co-leader of a very important and powerful party. After that, he was the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Switzerland, and after that he had the same position in London. From his book, I took out some of the most important parts which show us what he speaks and thinks about the facts, and whether his words tally with my words and my conclusions. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As I've already said it, the document is now 3D03554. General, I'm going to ask you, as you turn to a different page, give me its number, and I'll then call for the same page in the electronic courtroom. "I Was Alija's Diplomat" is the title of the book that we're going to discuss. It speaks of the time between 1991 and the end of the war, the time that is relevant for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Go ahead and tell us what you will about this book.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll take things at a time, and I am going to follow the instructions of the Trial Chamber, especially His Honour Judge Antonetti and I'm not going to read; I'm just going to comment, and I'm just going to paraphrase his words and his claims and what he claims you can find in the text. Can you please turn to page 12 in the Croatian or, rather, Bosniak text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0821 is the Croatian version, and in the English the same page bears the number 3D41-0867.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the introduction, he says -- or, rather, asks who is it who is responsible for -- or, rather, who bears the responsibility for Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he says that regardless of everybody else, in his view the leadership and intellectuals of Bosnia-Herzegovina bear a huge responsibility for what happened to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He also says that, and that's the next thing in the book, but we are still talking about the introduction, he says that his testimony will be reduced only to the events that he, himself, testified or that he participated in actively.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I apologise. In Croatian, it is 3D41-0822, and in the English it is the same page, 3D41-0867. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says further on that Alija Izetbegovic was de jure and de facto head of the state and that he remained so throughout the war. And he says that his policy resulted in the semi-colonial protectorate of the foreign forces, and that's how it was while he was writing his book. Further on, he says that in 1991, he visited Croatia and Slovenia, that he was one of the leaders of the Muslim Bosniak organisation, that he participated in the negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs in July and August 1991, and we will see that this was done at the initiative and with the approval of Mr. Izetbegovic. And then he goes on to speak about the conference in London, and he says that in winter of 1990, that's page 16 of Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is 3D41-0823 in the Croatian version and 3D41-0868 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He goes on to say that in 1993, he became -- or, rather, he stopped -- the diplomatic representative offices stopped when the union of three states within Bosnia-Herzegovina came into existence. In the winter of 1993, he was not a part of the negotiations on peace and became Bosnia-Herzegovina's ambassador to Switzerland, and then afterwards in London until 1996, when he was removed from those positions. Now we can move on to page 32 of the Bosniak text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D41-0824 of the Croatian, and 3D41-0868 of the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, he briefly refers to history. I'm not going to go into that, but it's interesting to see what he says about the system in which he lived from 1953, and the situation around Djilas. I don't want to burden the Judges about that unless they want to ask something about it. And then something I referred to later on, and said that the culmination of political violence against the Croats occurred during the Croatian Spring, as it was known, in 1971, when the political leadership was replaced, a legal, political, and state leadership was replaced and destroyed, and this partially also happened to a liberal leadership in Serbia. And I'm going on to page 33 now, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm paying attention to the pages. It's still on the same page, actually.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he goes into a very valid analysis of how the desires for greater freedom burgeoned and a different type of organisation for the economy and the country, and this went -- took a nationalistic course because it couldn't be resolved -- the question couldn't be resolved in any other way. And then he goes on to page 36 of the Bosniak text.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D41-0852 of the Croatian version, and 3D41-0868 for the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, he says that even if there was certain indecisions about what the programme of Slobodan Milosevic and Serbian thinking was, after his speech which he delivered at Gazimestan in Kosovo on the 28th of June, 1989, even a blind man would have seen that the programme had been developed and became an all-out war against the alleged anti-Serbs, and everything ended in bloodshed. And he states quite clearly something else that is important for all those dealing with the question of how history is shaped; that Milosevic came to lead not because he imposed himself on others, but because the political powers that be, the intellectual forces and circles in Serbia, needed him for the realisation of their programme, which was developed in the memorandum within the Serbian Academy of Arts and Science, known as the SANU. And then he goes on to say that for a long time, even during the first Yugoslavia and before the establishment of the first Yugoslavia, that the Serbs had not completed what they set out to do; that is to say, the unification of all Serb lands into a single Serbian state. And they defined what they considered to be theirs, and I quote, "all lands where Serb graves exist are Serb lands," or the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, which means up to Karlobag and Virovitica, which is the map that we've seen so many times before here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. This is 3D41-0869 in the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
